newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's new government attracts powerful guests.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's new government attracts powerful guests.

text.p: A more outward-looking government in Sofia is attracting a string of prominent visitors who feel Bulgaria's new leaders are people they can do business with, whether literally or in the political sense.

European Union External Affairs commissioner Hans van den Broek visited on Tuesday, preceded by U.S. Undersecretary of defence for policy Walter Slocombe on Monday, and a big Russian delegation last week led by the then deputy prime minister Oleg Lobov. German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel is due next week.
"I am confident that Bulgaria has rejoined the mainstream of political life in Europe, to the pleasure of its many friends," van den Broek said during his visit.

The wooing of Bulgaria is prompted as much by its relative stability in a volatile region as by interest in its potential as a strategically-sited transit point for road, rail and telephone traffic and natural gas.
"We have a strategy to help promote security in the region. It is to work with countries like Bulgaria that are forces for stability in the Balkans," Slocombe said.
Van den Broek also praised Bulgaria's political stability, but stressed its economic potential.
"At the intersection of major north-south and east-west routes, opportunities for Bulgaria abound in trade, transport and the development of oil and gas pipelines," he said.

President Petar Stoyanov won presidential elections last November as the candidate of the Union of Democratic Forces, which led 30 days of mass protests that toppled the Socialist government last month and is expected to win a majority in the next parliament.
U.S. economist Jeffrey Sachs, director of the Harvard Institute of Development and an advisor to Stoyanov, advised Bulgaria to make the most of its 15 minutes of fame.
"The Bulgarians are keen on having as many foreign guests as possible," said one diplomat. "One does have the impression that the UDF is mobilising the great and the good ahead of the elections."

Neighbouring Romania won similar attention after Emil Constantinescu won presidential elections last year and now has backing from Spain, France and Italy for a place in the first wave of NATO expansion.

The United States and Bulgaria's traditional ally Russia are deeply divided over NATO expansion. Slocombe's visit came as Presidents Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin prepared for a summit in Helsinki on Thursday and Friday.

One of the first decisions of the new interim cabinet was to make a clear statement of Bulgaria's desire to join NATO, an issue on which the Socialists had always been ambivalent for fear of upsetting their traditional allies in Moscow.
Stoyanov made his first overseas trip to Brussels, within days of taking office.
The former Socialist government, ousted last month after 30 days of mass protests, never got on particularly well with either Russia or the West.

It dragged its feet over granting big pipeline concessions for transporting Russian natural gas to Balkan countries, sought by Bulgarian-Russian joint stock company Topenergy, in which Russia's Gazprom and powerful Bulgarian conglomerate Multigroup both have stakes.
Bulgaria's interim government agreed with Lobov's delegation to cancel the Socialist government's concession procedure and prepare an alternative.

Lobov said last week that Russia would invest $600 million in the gas transit pipeline project and would also pay "large amounts in foreign currency" in transit fees. The pipeline would also guarantee Bulgarian energy supplies.

Bulgaria has little hope of entering the European Union or NATO in the first wave of eastern expansion, but with an eye on Albania and Serbia, both groups are keen to keep it in their sphere of influence.

"Bulgaria is an excellent example of how important it is to entertain good neighbourly relations, to be a pole of stability in the region and to enhance co-operation with its neighbours," van den Broek said. "We would like to see new members form a stable community."
